prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I keep B030 alone, credited to Katori and Ye, and my configuration is unchanged from round 1. What the exchange added is a sharper answer to the chair's first question. In one sentence: the 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb as a ruler and the 2012 prize honoured quantum control of individual trapped systems, whereas the lattice clock is a separate idea, a magic-wavelength optical lattice in which the trapping light does not shift the clock transition, so that thousands of neutral atoms are interrogated with ion-like accuracy. Round 1 showed that seven of eight members reach this configuration from different directions, but I do not count that as the argument. The argument is that the proposal is original, the realization was driven to a precision no one had before, and independent national laboratories reproduce clocks agreeing near 1e-18. I judge it as I would a new microscope principle: a concept, a working instrument, and then independent groups obtaining the same performance. On the citation, I now favour the third scope in the round-1 files, which names the magic-wavelength lattice, over my own bare round-1 wording. Naming the concept makes it clear that the award is for the lattice clock and not for optical clocks or timekeeping in general, and that is the best defence against the overlap worry. The citation should say nothing about the redefinition of the second, since the case rests on demonstrated performance alone.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes remains the strongest reservation, and Mehlig is right that the methods (laser cooling, trapping, precision spectroscopy) are close enough that a one-sentence distinction does not make the objection disappear for everyone. I think it is answerable but it is a judgement about novelty, not a fact. The credit boundary is the second weakness: Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Hinkley, Ushijima and the ion-clock groups contributed to accuracy and stability, and I cannot show from the supplied text that Katori for the proposal and early demonstrations and Ye for record accuracy, many-body clock physics and comparison technology is the only defensible two-name history. Pearce asked that this be called a judgement and I agree. Third, some of the case is still prospective, because the second has not been redefined and a critic can say the strongest payoff is pending. I accept that the committee must be willing to defend the pair against experts in the metrology community, and I do not claim more certainty than I have.

responses.point: Mehlig said the 2005 and 2012 citations are close enough in method that the overlap question is not closed, and asked that the citation stress neutral atoms trapped at the magic wavelength and interrogated as large ensembles.
responses.response: I agree with your drafting point and have changed my citation because of it. My round-1 wording, a bare invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, left room for a reader to hear metrology in general. Naming the magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms puts the novelty in the text. I do not agree that method overlap makes the question open in the sense of disqualifying: laser cooling and spectroscopy are the common toolbox, but the 2005 and 2012 citations do not contain the idea that the lattice can be made harmless to the clock transition. If you still think the overlap is disqualifying even with that wording, I would like to know what further wording or evidence would change your mind.

responses.point: Pearce asked Kroll to say plainly that the Katori and Ye allocation is a judgement and not a clean fact, since Lemonde, Ludlow and others are not a footnote.
responses.response: I agree and I will say it for myself. The allocation rests on a reading of the record that Katori holds the conceptual origin and early demonstrations and Ye the decisive demonstration of ultimate performance and the many-body and comparison work. It is a defensible reading, not a clean fact, and the committee should record it as such. I would add that I regard Lemonde and others as contested rather than clearly excluded, so I would not write the citation in a way that implies they did nothing. Because you now prefer B030 yourself, I also take it that your remaining concern is the citation scope and not the pair.

responses.point: Eriksson replied to my round-1 argument that instruments and devices qualify by saying B025 and B008 carry credit problems of their own, that nobody else ranked B025, and that if instruments qualify then a simulation method qualifies too.
responses.response: You are right on the facts and I concede both points. B025 has the missing Krivanek line and the TEM and STEM split, B008 has Kazarinov and Suris priority and the other Bell Labs co-authors, and B025 received no support beyond mine, so I withdraw both from my preferred configuration and will not argue for them. I also accept your logic that if invention counts, B022 cannot be excluded merely because it is a method, and I regard the physics-versus-chemistry question on B022 as unresolved and not as a disqualification. Where I still differ from you is on ranking: the Car and Parrinello credit is clean, but with only two members placing B022 in their top eight and a single prize part, I do not see a scientific reason to prefer it over B030, which has the same attribution clarity and a measurable performance record.

responses.point: Danielsson moved to B030 but asked that the citation state what the clocks have enabled, otherwise the metrology-overlap objection stays open, and holds that the discovery content must be argued through tests of redshift, constants and dark matter.
responses.response: I agree with the aim but would meet it differently. A citation that lists applications ties the prize to what the clocks may find next, whereas the physics we reward is already done: the light-shift cancellation, the forbidden-transition and many-body control, and the demonstration of agreement near 1e-18 between independent laboratories. For that reason I put the 1e-18 level in the citation but not the downstream tests; the redshift, constants and dark-matter results belong in the scientific background document where they show the clock changed what can be measured. If you think the citation must name the enabled physics to survive the overlap objection, I would like to hear which phrase you would use.

responses.point: Lindroth would not name Lemonde in the citation and would not lean on the redefinition of the second, and asked whether the credit can survive scrutiny from experts in the metrology community.
responses.response: On the redefinition, we agree and the citation should rest on what has been measured. On Lemonde, I would not name him either, since the citation is limited to the concept and its realization and a prize cannot name more than three people, but I would not write a rationale that dismisses the work of other lattice-clock groups. Whether the pair survives expert scrutiny is a fair test that none of us can fully run from the supplied files. I would support seeking outside advice in the usual way before the vote is final, and I would change my view of the pair only if a concrete priority record contradicted Katori's proposal or Ye's realization role.

uncertainties: Whether members who hold the overlap worry (Mehlig, Danielsson, Johansson, Pearce) will treat the one-sentence distinction between a magic-wavelength lattice clock and the 2005 and 2012 prizes as sufficient.
Whether the Katori and Ye pair would hold up against detailed priority records for Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups, which I cannot verify from the supplied files.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second will be read by some colleagues as a reason to wait; I do not think it is, but I cannot rule it out.

My two alternatives, B004 and B058, are chosen as the most widely supported fallbacks, and both have unresolved credit questions within three names (Greiner and Esslinger for B004, the choice of three for B058); I have not independently verified those priority details.
statement.conflict_note: B025 (aberration-corrected electron optics) is in my own field of transmission electron microscopy. I have withdrawn it from my configuration and would recuse myself from any decision that weighs it. For B030 I have long-running academic exchanges with Japanese universities, including a University of Tokyo fellowship, but no specific connection to Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. Göran Johansson is also at Chalmers; his B029 is not in my configuration, and I see no conflict with B030 or my alternatives B004 and B058.
